events.text: Jekyll recounts being born to a large fortune and excellent parts.
events.quote: I was born in the year 18— to a large fortune, endowed besides with excellent parts

events.text: He conceals his pleasures and commits to a profound duplicity of life.
events.quote: I concealed my pleasures; and that when I reached years of reflection

events.text: He concludes man is not truly one but truly two.
events.quote: that man is not truly one, but truly two

events.text: He daydreams of separating his good and evil elements into separate identities.
events.quote: I had learned to dwell with pleasure, as a beloved daydream, on the thought of the separation of these elements

events.text: A side light from the laboratory table reveals the transience of the body.
events.quote: a side light began to shine upon the subject from the laboratory table

events.text: He compounds a drug to dethrone his powers and substitute a second form.
events.quote: managed to compound a drug by which these powers should be dethroned from their supremacy

events.text: He hesitates long, knowing he risks death, before testing the theory.
events.quote: I hesitated long before I put this theory to the test of practice

events.text: He buys a large quantity of a particular salt from wholesale chemists.
events.quote: I purchased at once, from a firm of wholesale chemists, a large quantity of a particular salt

events.text: Late one accursed night he compounds the elements and drinks the potion.
events.quote: late one accursed night, I compounded the elements

events.text: Racking pangs and deadly nausea succeed before the agonies subside.
events.quote: The most racking pangs succeeded: a grinding in the bones, deadly nausea

events.text: He feels younger, lighter, happier, and conscious of heady recklessness.
events.quote: I felt younger, lighter, happier in body

events.text: He realizes he has lost in stature.
events.quote: I was suddenly aware that I had lost in stature

events.text: He ventures in his new shape through the house toward his bedroom.
events.quote: I determined, flushed as I was with hope and triumph, to venture in my new shape as far as to my bedroom

events.text: He sees for the first time the appearance of Edward Hyde.

relation_context.story_before_this_passage:
During a Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at a sinister door. Enfield recalls Hyde trampling a girl, then paying her family £100 with a genuine cheque. Utterson studies Jekyll’s will, which leaves everything to Hyde if Jekyll vanishes. Lanyon says Jekyll grew too fanciful and has never heard of Hyde. Keeping watch, Utterson accosts Hyde, who admits Jekyll is out, gives a Soho address, then snarls and disappears inside. Poole confirms Hyde has a key and all servants must obey him. Jekyll pales when Utterson mentions Hyde, refuses more, but says he can be rid of Hyde whenever he chooses. He asks Utterson to help Hyde for his sake when gone.

A maid saw Hyde cane Sir Danvers Carew to death. The mangled body bore a sealed envelope for Utterson, who identified Carew. Inspector Newcomen showed the broken stick, which Utterson recognized as Jekyll’s gift. They searched Hyde’s rooms, finding the other half and a burnt cheque book. Hyde had thousands at the bank, but few familiars, no photograph, and wildly differing descriptions.

Poole admits Utterson to Jekyll’s cabinet. Jekyll swears he will never see Hyde again. Jekyll gives Utterson a letter signed Edward Hyde, saying he burned the envelope, which had no postmark, and that Hyde dictated his will. Poole says no letter came except by post. Guest finds the murderer’s letter identical to Jekyll’s note. Utterson locks it in his safe, suspecting forgery.

After the murder, Hyde vanishes and rewards are offered. Jekyll resumes old friendships, then shuts his door; Poole says he is confined. Utterson finds Lanyon decayed, doomed, refusing Jekyll’s name. ut the glass to his lips and drank at one gulp. A cry followed; he reeled, staggered, clutched at the table and held on, staring with injected eyes, gasping with open mouth; and as I looked there came, I thought, a change—he seemed to swell—his face became suddenly black and the features seemed to melt and alter—and the next moment, I had sprung to my feet and leaped back against the wall, my arms raised to shield me from that prodigy, my mind submerged in terror.
[P17] “O God!” I screamed, and “O God!” again and again; for there before my eyes—pale and shaken, and half fainting, and groping before him with his hands, like a man restored from death—there stood Henry Jekyll!
[P18] What he told me in the next hour, I cannot bring my mind to set on paper. I saw what I saw, I heard what I heard, and my soul sickened at it; and yet now when that sight has faded from my eyes, I ask myself if I believe it, and I cannot answer. My life is shaken to its roots; sleep has left me; the deadliest terror sits by me at all hours of the day and night; and I feel that my days are numbered, and that I must die; and yet I shall die incredulous. As for the moral turpitude that man unveiled to me, even with tears of penitence, I cannot, even in memory, dwell on it without a start of horror. I will say but one thing, Utterson, and that (if you can bring your mind to credit it) will be more than enough. The creature who crept into my house that night was, on Jekyll’s own confession, known by the name of Hyde and hunted for in every corner of the land as the murderer of Carew.
[P19] HASTIE LANYON.

known_before.bio: Henry Jekyll is a fifty-year-old doctor, colleague of Dr. Lanyon, and lawyer Utterson's acquaintance, known for charities and religion. He is hunted across the land as Carew's murderer. He swore never to set eyes on Hyde again, admitted Hyde dictated his will, and after Hyde vanished resumed his old friendships. He then shut his door against Utterson, vowed extreme seclusion, and spoke of an unnameable punishment.
